x.ASV: A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. O God, thou art my God; earnestly will I seek thee: My soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee, In a dry and weary land, where no water is.
x.Darby: A Psalm of David; when he was in the wilderness of Judah. OGod, thou art myGod; early will I seek thee. My soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh languisheth for thee, in a dry and weary land without water:
x.KJV: A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is;
x.YLT: A Psalm of David, in his being in the wilderness of Judah. O God, Thou art my God, earnestly do I seek Thee, Thirsted for Thee hath my soul, Longed for Thee hath my flesh, In a land dry and weary, without waters.

nt: David is speaking of his intense desire for God as if his **soul** were physically **thirsting** for water. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My soul longs for you] or [I deeply desire to be near you]
David is using **My soul** to represent all of himself in the act of thirsting for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I thirst]

The psalmist is speaking of his intense longing for God as if his body were physically **fainting** from weakness or exhaustion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my whole being aches for you] or [my body grows weak with longing for you]

David is using one part of a person, his **flesh**, to mean all of him in the act of longing for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my whole being faints for you] or [I faint for you]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [My whole being longs for you]

The terms **dryness** and **weary** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very dry] or [extremely parched]

x.ASV: So have I looked upon thee in the sanctuary, To see thy power and thy glory.
x.Darby: To see thy power and thy glory, as I have beheld thee in the sanctuary;
x.KJV: To see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary.
x.YLT: So in the sanctuary I have seen Thee, To behold Thy strength and Thine honour.

nt: The word translated as **Thus** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [So] or [Because of this,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how powerful you are]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how glorious you are]

The terms **power** and **glory** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [your awesome power] or [your magnificent strength]

x.ASV: Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, My lips shall praise thee.
x.Darby: For thy loving-kindness is better than life: my lips shall praise thee.
x.KJV: Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee.
x.YLT: Because better is Thy kindness than life, My lips do praise Thee.

nt: The word translated as **Because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came after. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came after. Alternate translation: [Since]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how faithful you are to your covenant] or [how faithfully you keep your covenant promises]

The psalmist says **better than life** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [more valuable than anything] or [extremely valuable]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **lips**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will praise you]

x.ASV: So will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name.
x.Darby: So will I bless thee while I live; I will lift up my hands in thy name.
x.KJV: Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name.
x.YLT: So I bless Thee in my life, in Thy name I lift up my hands.

nt: The word **Thus** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. David will bless God because of what he has just expressed in the previous verses. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because of this,] or [Therefore,]

Lifting up one’s palms was a symbolic action by which David showed his worship and prayer to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I will lift up my palms to worship you] or [I will lift up my palms in prayer to you]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who God is, particularly God’s character and authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of who you are] or [because of your character]

x.ASV: My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; And my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips;
x.Darby: My soul is satisfied as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise [thee] with joyful lips.
x.KJV: My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips:
x.YLT: As with milk and fatness is my soul satisfied, And with singing lips doth my mouth praise.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **fat and fatness** are deeply satisfying, so God’s presence satisfies the psalmist’s soul. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My soul will be completely satisfied, just as if I had eaten the richest foods]

The terms **fat** and **fatness** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the richest food]

By using the phrase **my soul will be full**, David is speaking as if Yahweh could satisfy him in the same way that rich food satisfies hunger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [I will be as satisfied as if I had eaten the richest foods]
David is using **my soul** to represent all of himself in the act of being satisfied. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **lips**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with my joyful shouts]

Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. David is using one part of a person, his **mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

x.ASV: When I remember thee upon my bed, And meditate on thee in the night-watches.
x.Darby: When I remember thee upon my bed, I meditate on thee in the night-watches:
x.KJV: When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.
x.YLT: If I have remembered Thee on my couch, In the watches--I meditate on Thee.

nt: The word **When** indicates that David **remembering** God occurred at the same time as when he **meditates** on God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [As I remember you on my bed]

The term **night watches** refers to the divisions of the night during which guards were on duty. In ancient Israel, the night was typically divided into three or four such periods. If your readers would not be familiar with this, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [during the night] or [in the hours of the night]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [When I remember you on my bed, yes, when I meditate on you in the night watches]

x.ASV: For thou hast been my help, And in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice.
x.Darby: For thou hast been my help, and in the shadow of thy wings will I sing for joy.
x.KJV: Because thou hast been my help, therefore in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice.
x.YLT: For Thou hast been a help to me, And in the shadow of Thy wings I sing.

nt: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because] or [Since]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [one who gives help] or [helpful]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a bird protecting him **in the shadow of** his **wings**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while you protect me] or [as you shelter me]

David is speaking of God as if he had **wings** that cast a shadow providing protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your protective shelter] or [your protection]

x.ASV: My soul followeth hard after thee: Thy right hand upholdeth me.
x.Darby: My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me.
x.KJV: My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me.
x.YLT: Cleaved hath my soul after Thee, On me hath Thy right hand taken hold.

nt: David is using **My soul** to represent all of himself in the act of clinging to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

David is speaking of his devotion to God as if his soul physically **clings** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [remains devoted to you] or [holds tightly to you]

Here, **right hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your strength]

x.ASV: But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, Shall go into the lower parts of the earth.
x.Darby: But those that seek my soul, to destroy [it], shall go into the lower parts of the earth;
x.KJV: But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth.
x.YLT: And they who for desolation seek my soul, Go in to the lower parts of the earth.

nt: The psalmist is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they seek** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that his enemies seek his life. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But my enemies truly seek]

The pronoun **they** refers to David’s enemies, who have not been mentioned previously in this psalm. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But those who are my enemies]
David is using **my life** to represent his entire person in the act being killed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to kill me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **devastation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to destroy me]

David is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **the lowest parts of the earth**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [to the grave] or [to Sheol]

x.ASV: They shall be given over to the power of the sword: They shall be a portion for foxes.
x.Darby: They shall be given over to the power of the sword; they shall be the portion of foxes.
x.KJV: They shall fall by the sword: they shall be a portion for foxes.
x.YLT: They cause him to run on the edge of the sword, A portion for foxes they are.

nt: The psalmist is using **pour him into the hands of the sword** as a common expression of the culture to mean “cause him to be killed by the sword.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will hand him over to be slain by the sword] or [They will cause him to die by the sword]

The psalmist is speaking of **the sword** as if it were a living thing that could have **hands**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the destructive power of the sword] or [death by the sword]

The psalmist is speaking of his enemies’ dead bodies as if they were **a portion of jackals**, that is, food that would be given to scavenging animals. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will become food for wild animals]

A **jackal** is a kind of wild scavenging animal. If your readers would not be familiar with what a jackal is, you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [scavengers]

The pronoun **him** is singular, but it refers to the psalmist’s enemies, who are plural. David may be referring to them collectively. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a plural form. Alternate translation: [them]

x.ASV: But the king shall rejoice in God: Every one that sweareth by him shall glory; For the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped.
x.Darby: But the king shall rejoice inGod; every one that sweareth by him shall glory: for the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped.
x.KJV: But the king shall rejoice in God; every one that sweareth by him shall glory: but the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped.
x.YLT: And the king doth rejoice in God, Boast himself doth every one swearing by Him, But stopped is the mouth of those speaking lies!

nt: By **the king**, David means himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I, the king,]
The pronoun **him** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [by God]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, **the mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of speaking lies. The phrase **will be shut** means that they will be stopped or silenced. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [speakers of falsehood will be silenced] or [those who speak falsehood will be stopped]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [false things]

The expression **will be shut** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will shut the mouth of speakers of falsehood] or [will stop speaking]
